related.note: The resolution welcomes the Pact for the Future and the Global Digital Compact, including their commitment to international human-rights law throughout the life cycle of digital and emerging technologies.
The resolution welcomes the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July 2026 and takes note of the Independent International Scientific Panel's preliminary report.
The resolution recalls the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (23 November 2021).
CETS 225 is the binding AI-specific human-rights treaty; the HRC resolution is universal but non-binding.
Earlier UNGA AI resolution; the HRC resolution builds on the UN's AI-governance track.

ai_provisions: Operative paragraph 1 — recognises AI's potential to contribute to human rights and sustainable development, while acknowledging risks to the enjoyment of human rights.

Operative paragraph 2 — affirms that the design, development, deployment and use of AI must be consistent with international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law as applicable.

Operative paragraphs 3–7 — AI governance under human-rights law; legislative and regulatory measures; participation of developing countries; access to information; human dignity, equality, privacy, transparency, explainability, accountability, accessibility, human oversight and effective remedies.

Operative paragraph 8 — States should refrain from or cease uses of AI that cannot be operated consistently with international human rights law or that pose undue risks, including systems whose capabilities could reasonably be expected to cause loss of human control.

Operative paragraphs 9–10 — human-rights due diligence and impact assessments; meaningful human oversight, information, human review and effective remedies where AI plays a material role in decisions affecting rights.

Operative paragraphs 11–13 — freedom of opinion and expression, privacy, differentiated impacts on vulnerable groups, and the responsibility of business enterprises under the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
Operative paragraphs 14–17 — AI literacy, international cooperation and capacity building, digital public goods and open models, and coherence among international initiatives.
Operative paragraphs 20–23 — a panel discussion at the 65th session on AI capacity building and the AI divide; an OHCHR report to the 66th session; the Council remains seized of the matter.
relevance.excluded_scope: A non-binding Human Rights Council resolution. It creates no signature, ratification, depositary, monitoring or enforcement mechanism, and it does not establish a military-AI prohibition. It applies existing human-rights obligations rather than creating new ones.
relevance.reason: A dedicated Human Rights Council resolution on the human-rights implications of artificial intelligence, adopted without a vote on 6 October 2026. It complements the General Assembly resolutions and CETS 225 by applying existing international human-rights law across the AI life cycle: discrimination, privacy, freedom of expression, human oversight, due diligence, remedies and capacity building. It is non-binding and creates no enforcement mechanism, but it is the Human Rights Council's principal AI-specific text and was missing from the corpus.
